subject: Archaeology
title: Open Access and Data Sharing
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Open Access and Data Sharing.

hook.text: Most archaeological data was locked in filing cabinets. Open access is changing that.

buildup.text: Decades of dig data sat behind expensive journal paywalls, inaccessible to most.

discovery.text: Platforms like tDAR and ADS host millions of records freely available to anyone.

twist.text: Some archaeologists resist sharing data, fearing others will publish first.

climax.text: Funding bodies now require open data as a grant condition. The culture is shifting.

punchline.text: The data was always there. It just needed the internet to open it.

quiz.question: What slowed open data adoption in archaeology?
options: Privacy laws prevented sharing data about remains
Some feared others would publish from their data first
Digital storage was too expensive for institutions

details.summary: Open access in archaeology means making research data, publications, and 3D models freely available online. Digital repositories and open journals allow researchers worldwide to access excavation records, artifact databases, and site reports without expensive institutional subscriptions.
details.whyItMatters: Most archaeological research has been locked behind paywalls and institutional archives. Open access democratizes knowledge, enables verification of claims, and allows researchers in less wealthy countries to participate fully in global archaeology.
takeaways: Open access removes paywalls from archaeological publications
Digital repositories share excavation data and 3D artifact models
It enables global participation regardless of institutional wealth

faq.question: What are the main open access platforms for archaeology?
faq.answer: The Archaeology Data Service, tDAR (the Digital Archaeological Record), Open Context, and MorphoSource for 3D models are major platforms. Open-access journals like Internet Archaeology and Advances in Archaeological Practice publish peer-reviewed research without paywalls.

faq.question: Why do some archaeologists resist open data sharing?
faq.answer: Concerns include protecting sensitive site locations from looters, respecting indigenous communities' control over their cultural data, and researchers wanting to publish their findings first. Balancing openness with these legitimate concerns requires nuanced data sharing policies.
